title: The Gap in Zero to n
statement:
You get an array nums of length n. Its values are distinct and come from the range 0 to n inclusive. That range has n + 1 values, so exactly one of them is not in the array.

Return the missing value. Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra memory.

examples.why: n = 4, so the range is 0 to 4. Only 3 is absent.
n = 3 and the missing value is n itself. A scan for the first gap in sorted order finds none, so it must fall back to returning n.
n = 1, range 0 to 1. The missing value is 0, which is easy to lose if 0 is also your "nothing found" result or your starting point.

hints: You know exactly which values should be there. What can you compute about the full range 0..n without looking at the array?
The full range sums to n(n + 1) / 2. Subtract the array's sum and see what is left. Then think of XOR: what happens if you XOR every index and every value together?
XOR all of 0..n with all values in the array. Each present value appears twice and cancels; the missing one appears once and remains.

explain.intuition:
You know exactly what the complete set should look like: 0, 1, …, n. Compare a summary of the complete set with the same summary of the array, and the difference is the missing value.

Sum version: the full range sums to n(n + 1) / 2. Subtract the array's sum and the missing value is what remains. In JavaScript or Python this is safe, but in fixed-width languages n(n + 1) / 2 overflows a 32-bit int once n passes about 65 000. XOR version: XOR every number 0..n with every value in the array. Present values appear twice and cancel (a ^ a = 0), and the missing value appears once and survives. XOR never overflows, which is why it is the version interviewers like. The loop index covers 0..n−1, so start the accumulator at n to include the last one.
steps: Set acc = n (the array's length), which covers the top of the range.
Return acc. Every value present was XOR-ed in twice, once as an index or n, once as a value.
pitfalls: Sorting and looking for the first nums[i] !== i, then forgetting the case where the missing value is n and no gap is found.
Starting the XOR accumulator at 0 and looping only over indices 0..n−1. The value n is never included, so the answer is wrong whenever n is present.
Using the sum formula with 32-bit ints in C, Java or Go: n(n + 1) overflows for large n. Compute it in 64 bits or use XOR.

solutions.title: Check every candidate
solutions.idea: For each value 0..n, scan the array for it. The first one not found is the answer.

solutions.title: Expected sum minus actual sum
solutions.idea: 0 + 1 + … + n = n(n + 1) / 2. Subtract the array's sum. Safe in JS and Python; overflows 32-bit ints elsewhere.

solutions.title: XOR indices and values
solutions.idea: XOR every number in 0..n with every array value. Pairs cancel; the missing value is left. No overflow risk.

followups: The array is already sorted. Can you beat O(n)?
Two values are missing from 0..n. How do the sum and the sum of squares, or XOR plus one splitting bit, find both?
